arc_intro:
FQ-156 — Priya Nair (Cloud Architect)

Last piece of this ticket. Right now foodquick.in doesn't actually exist as far as AWS is concerned — the mobile app is hardcoded to call foodquick-alb-1a2b3c4d5e.ap-south-1.elb.amazonaws.com directly. If that ALB is ever recreated for any reason, that name changes, and the app breaks instantly for every user, everywhere, with no way to fix it without an app store release.

Set up a real hosted zone for foodquick.in. And Ravi mentioned he wants to canary a new checkout flow soon — a small percentage of traffic first, not everyone at once — so keep routing policies in mind while you're in there, not just the domain itself.

— Priya
arc_outro:
Priya Nair — FQ-156 update:

foodquick.in is live and correctly configured — ALIAS at the apex, CNAME where it actually belongs, weighted routing ready for Ravi's canary rollout, and a real failover path with health checks if the primary ever goes down. The mobile app can be updated to use the real domain instead of the raw ALB name whenever the app team is ready.

I want to say something now that this ticket's actually closing: what started as 'clean up the network' turned into understanding this VPC was never actually designed — and by the end, you traced an 8-month-old mystery back to a cancelled delivery pilot nobody finished cleaning up after. That's the real work. Every piece of this network is now something you understand, not something you inherited blind.

Ravi's going to loop you in on FQ-171 next — compute's been sized on guesses since day one, and it shows. See you there.

— Priya

tasks.question: What's the real risk of the mobile app hardcoding the ALB's own auto-generated DNS name instead of a custom domain?

C) The only risk is slightly worse performance compared to using a custom domain
D) Raw ALB DNS names cost extra money to use, unlike custom domains

tasks.scenario: You're about to add the record for the apex domain (foodquick.in, no www) pointing to the ALB. karthik-dev suggests using a CNAME, same as you're about to do for www.foodquick.in.
tasks.question: Can foodquick.in (the apex/root domain itself) use a CNAME record, the same way www.foodquick.in does?
options: A) Yes — CNAME works identically at the apex and at any subdomain

B) No — DNS specifications don't allow a CNAME record to exist at the zone apex, because the apex must also hold other required record types (like NS and SOA records), and a CNAME can't coexist with other records on the same name. Route 53's ALIAS record type exists specifically to solve this — it behaves like a CNAME but is allowed at the apex
C) No — the apex domain can never point to an ALB under any circumstances, only to a fixed IP address
D) Yes, but only if the hosted zone is configured in 'legacy mode'

tasks.error_shown: An error occurred (InvalidChangeBatch) when calling the ChangeResourceRecordSets operation: RRSet of type CNAME with DNS name foodquick.in. is not permitted at apex in zone foodquick.in.
tasks.diagnosis: This is exactly the DNS apex restriction from the previous task, now hit as a real API error instead of a hypothetical. Route 53 is enforcing the same rule every DNS provider does — a CNAME cannot exist at the zone apex alongside the zone's own required NS and SOA records.
tasks.fix: Delete the failed CNAME attempt and create an ALIAS record instead for foodquick.in, targeting the ALB. ALIAS records are a Route 53-specific feature that behave like a CNAME (resolving to the ALB's current address) but ARE permitted at the zone apex.

tasks.scenario: Ravi is ready to canary the new checkout flow: 'Send about 10% of traffic to the new checkout-service-v2 endpoint, and keep 90% on the existing checkout-service-v1. I want to watch error rates before we go further.'
tasks.question: Which Route 53 routing policy fits this requirement?
options: A) Simple routing — it always returns the same single answer, with no way to split traffic by percentage

B) Weighted routing — you assign a relative weight to each record (e.g. 90 and 10), and Route 53 returns each answer roughly in that proportion, which is exactly the gradual-canary pattern being asked for
C) Latency-based routing — this routes based on which endpoint is geographically closest/fastest for the user, not based on any percentage split
D) Failover routing — this only ever sends traffic to a backup when the primary is unhealthy, it doesn't do a percentage split

tasks.scenario: Separately, Priya wants a failover path: if the primary ALB in ap-south-1 ever becomes unhealthy, foodquick.in should automatically start resolving to a backup static maintenance page hosted in S3, instead of leaving users staring at a broken app.
tasks.question: What does Route 53 need, beyond just a failover routing policy, to actually know WHEN to switch to the backup?
options: A) Nothing else — failover routing policies automatically detect ALB health with no additional configuration

B) A Route 53 Health Check — configured to periodically check the primary ALB's health endpoint (e.g. /health); Route 53 uses the health check's pass/fail status to decide whether to keep serving the primary record or switch to the secondary
C) A CloudWatch Alarm is the only way to trigger DNS failover — Route 53 has no health-checking feature of its own
D) Failover routing works purely based on which record was created first, not on any health signal

tasks.scenario: Priya asks you to match the right Route 53 routing policy to three different future scenarios FoodQuick is likely to face as it grows.

cases.case_1: FoodQuick expands to serve customers from both ap-south-1 (Mumbai) and a new ap-southeast-1 (Singapore) region, and wants each user automatically served from whichever region responds fastest for them
cases.case_2: FoodQuick wants to gradually roll out a redesigned home page to a small percentage of users first, watching metrics before a full rollout
cases.case_3: FoodQuick wants automatic protection against an entire region going down, with traffic automatically shifting to the surviving region without any manual DNS changes

correct_answers.case_1: Latency-based routing — routes each user to whichever endpoint has the lowest latency for them specifically, ideal for genuinely multi-region setups serving different geographies
correct_answers.case_2: Weighted routing — same pattern as the checkout canary in this lesson, splitting traffic by percentage between the old and new versions
correct_answers.case_3: Failover routing with health checks on both regions — automatically shifts all traffic to the surviving region's endpoint the moment the primary region's health check fails, no manual intervention needed
